title: Not quite eye to A.I.: student and teacher perspectives on the use of generative artificial intelligence in the writing process
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper examines how students and teachers perceive the acceptable use of generative artificial intelligence, specifically ChatGPT, across different stages of the writing process. The core problem addressed is the lack of consensus about what constitutes appropriate versus inappropriate use of GenAI in education, especially given concerns about plagiarism, academic integrity, and the disruption caused by tools that can generate, revise, and evaluate text. The study asks how undergraduate students and teachers view GenAI use for brainstorming, outlining, writing, revising, feedback, and evaluation, and whether their views differ.

The study used a cross-sectional questionnaire design. Participants were shown example prompts and outputs from ChatGPT for six writing-related tasks and then rated the appropriateness of four forms of use: offloading a task the user already knows how to do, using AI output as a model for ideas, submitting AI-generated output with disclosure, and submitting it without disclosure. The instrument focused on student uses for brainstorming, outlining, writing, and revising, and teacher uses for feedback and evaluation. Analysis included response frequencies, Mann-Whitney U comparisons between teacher and student groups, exploratory factor analysis, and principal component analysis.

The population consisted primarily of 158 university students from a public research university in the United States and 68 teachers recruited across multiple institutions worldwide, mainly second-language teachers teaching at the adult/university level. A small minority of respondents included graduate students, non-language educators, and two K-12 teachers. Thus, the context is primarily higher education rather than secondary schooling, and the study measures perceptions rather than direct writing-performance outcomes.

The main conclusion is that both students and teachers generally view GenAI as more acceptable for supportive functions such as brainstorming, outlining, and modeling ideas than for directly producing or revising work that is submitted as one's own. Both groups especially disapproved of undisclosed AI use. Teachers were somewhat more accepting of AI as a model for feedback and evaluation, while students were somewhat more accepting of undisclosed or disclosed AI use in outlining, writing, and revision. The authors conclude that institutions need explicit AI-use guidelines, greater transparency norms, and substantially more teacher professional development, as most respondents reported little or no institutional policy or training on AI.
quality_tier_rationale: Peer-reviewed cross-sectional survey with clear methods and reported reliability, but it is not a causal design and the sample is non-random and primarily higher education, limiting relevance to K-12 intervention effects.
impact_tier_rationale: The study reports perceptions and institutional readiness rather than direct learning impacts; effects on educational outcomes are unclear, so practical impact for secondary writing performance cannot be established.

interventions.use_case: Survey-based evaluation of ChatGPT/genAI use across stages of the writing process, including brainstorming, outlining, drafting, revising, teacher feedback, and teacher evaluation.
Paper situates ChatGPT alongside AI writing/language tools for writing support and discusses its use as a writing assistant for revision and language improvement.
Teacher-oriented scenarios ask respondents to judge the appropriateness of using ChatGPT to generate formative feedback and evaluative comments on student writing.

finding.finding_summary: The survey found substantial institutional unpreparedness for generative AI use in writing education. Among teachers (n=68), 94.1% reported their institution did not have an AI policy, 95.6% reported receiving no AI training, and 89.7% had not educated students about appropriate AI use; student reports from one university (n=158) were mixed on whether an institutional policy existed. These findings indicate weak policy readiness and limited implementation support rather than measured learning effects.
finding.measure: Survey items on institutional AI policy, training provision, and whether teachers had educated students about appropriate AI use
finding.study_size: n=226 total; teachers n=68, students n=158

finding.finding_summary: Respondents generally perceived AI as useful for teacher work, especially teachers themselves. On the item 'AI will be a useful tool for teachers,' teachers reported higher agreement than students (teachers M=3.99, SD=0.74; students M=3.32, SD=1.18; Mann-Whitney U=7098, p<0.001), suggesting perceived productivity/workload benefits from AI-supported writing tasks such as feedback and evaluation. However, the study did not directly measure time savings or workload reduction.
finding.measure: Likert survey ratings of perceived usefulness of AI for teachers
finding.study_size: n=226 total; teachers n=68, students n=158

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not test writing-quality outcomes, revised drafts, or independent writing performance. Instead, it measures perceptions of acceptable ChatGPT use in the writing process among university students and teachers, so no direct literacy impact estimate is available.
finding.measure: Perception ratings about appropriateness of AI use for brainstorming, outlining, drafting, revising, feedback, and evaluation
finding.study_size: n=226 total; teachers n=68, students n=158
